about: What each place's law already says on a policy question when a game starts (2026). governing/law-in-force.ts reads it as law in force at its level (US is federal, US-XX is the state); an enacted law at the same or a higher level governs after it takes effect. A place that isn't listed for a question has no answer, which is unknown and never read as no. Dates are operative dates; a law with no date has been in force since before any game starts. A row may also carry cite (the statute or constitutional section), source (a page that supports it) and preempts: true where state law rules the question out for its cities (a preemption statute, or a question only the state answers), false where the state has no law on it and its cities may act.

effectiveDates.about: When a state law takes effect if the act names no date of its own, as in force on 1/1/2026. Each rule is read from the place's constitution or code, or, where marked estimated, taken from the most common rule among places like it (ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE). A rule that counts from a session's end reads it from sessionEnds, one table for every place: the day the legislature published as its adjournment for a year whose session has ended (adjourned, read 9/29/2026 for 2026), else the latest day its law lets the regular session run, estimated where the law sets no calendar limit. A rule that counts from final passage uses the date the game records for the act (Illinois). Acts that name their own date, emergency clauses, appropriation acts and special sessions are not modeled here.

US-AK.note: Laws take effect ninety days after enactment unless two-thirds of each house set another date.

US-AL.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the most common rule among the places whose rule was read, the day after ninety full days from the session's end (Arizona, Arkansas, Kentucky, Maine, Michigan, Texas and Washington), counted from the estimated session end.
US-AL.note: Read but not dated: No default found for ordinary acts; Alabama acts name their own date. Penal acts take effect 60 days after approval.

US-AR.cite: Ark. Const. art. 5, § 1 (Amend. 7); Ark. Att'y Gen. Op. No. 2021-029
US-AR.note: An act without an emergency clause takes effect on the 91st day after the session's final adjournment, the day after the 90-day referendum window closes (2019: adjourned April 24, effective July 24).

US-AS.cite: Rev. Const. of American Samoa art. II, § 19
US-AS.note: An act approved by the Governor takes effect "no sooner than 60 days from the end of the session"; the game uses the sixtieth day. No year's actual count was read.

US-AZ.note: No act is operative for ninety days after the session closes; acts take effect on the 91st day (2025: adjourned June 27, effective September 26).

US-CA.cite: Cal. Const. art. IV, § 8(c)(1)-(2); Cal. Gov. Code § 9600(a)
US-CA.note: A regular-session statute takes effect on the January 1 after a 90-day period from enactment (§ 8(c)(1), repeated in Gov. Code § 9600(a)). A bill passed before the first year's joint recess and signed after it takes effect the next January 1 (§ 8(c)(2)). The recess runs from September into January, so the game treats every act of the first year, an odd year, as taking effect the next January 1 (inferred from the recess, not stated in the text). Special sessions (91st day after adjournment) and a pending referendum petition are not modeled.

US-CO.note: An act that states no date takes effect on its passage; the game counts from enactment. Most Colorado acts state their own date, often after the 90-day referendum window in art. V, § 1(3).

US-CT.note: Public acts take effect on the October 1 after the session that passed them; special acts take effect on approval.

US-DC.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the most common rule among the places whose rule was read, the day after ninety full days from the session's end (Arizona, Arkansas, Kentucky, Maine, Michigan, Texas and Washington), counted from the estimated session end.
US-DC.note: Read but not dated: An act takes effect after 30 days of Congress's review (60 for criminal titles), counted in days Congress sits.

US-DE.cite: Delaware Legislative Drafting Manual (Division of Legislative Services)
US-DE.note: The legislature's own drafting manual says all bills enacted into law take effect immediately unless they say otherwise. No code section states it; 1 Del. C. § 102 dates only the Code itself.

US-FL.note: "Each law shall take effect on the sixtieth day after adjournment sine die ... or as otherwise provided therein." Most acts name their own date, usually July 1 or October 1.

US-GA.note: An act approved from January 1 through June 30 takes effect July 1; one approved from July 1 through December 31 takes effect the next January 1.

US-GU.note: A law takes effect at midnight of the day the governor approves it. A bill that becomes law unsigned takes effect at midnight on the tenth day (Sundays excepted), and an override on the day it is repassed.

US-HI.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the most common rule among the places whose rule was read, the day after ninety full days from the session's end (Arizona, Arkansas, Kentucky, Maine, Michigan, Texas and Washington), counted from the estimated session end.
US-HI.note: Read but not dated: Laws bind once printed and published; no number of days is set.

US-IA.note: Regular-session acts take effect on the July 1 after passage; an act passed before July 1 but approved on or after it takes effect 45 days after approval. The game counts both from enactment.

US-ID.note: July 1 of the session's year or 60 days after the session ends, whichever is later (2025: adjourned April 4, effective July 1).

US-IL.note: Counted from the legislature's final passage, which the enactment records: a bill passed before June 1 takes effect the next January 1, or on becoming law if that is later (§ 1); one passed after May 31 takes effect June 1 of the next year (§ 2). An act recorded before the game kept the passage date is not dated.

US-IN.note: Each section of a regular-session act takes effect on the July 1 after its enactment unless it names another time.

US-KS.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the most common rule among the places whose rule was read, the day after ninety full days from the session's end (Arizona, Arkansas, Kentucky, Maine, Michigan, Texas and Washington), counted from the estimated session end.
US-KS.note: Read but not dated: Acts take effect on publication in the session laws; the publication date was not read from the code.

US-KY.note: No act becomes law until ninety days after the session adjourns. The Attorney General leaves out the day of adjournment and dates acts from the day after the ninetieth: the 2026 session adjourned April 15, 2026, and its acts took effect July 15, 2026. So the rule is 91 days after the session's last day, which the session-end table gives as the latest the constitution allows (March 30 in odd years, April 15 in even years); a session that adjourned earlier is dated late by the difference.

US-LA.note: Regular-session laws take effect August 1 of the session's year. Extraordinary-session laws take effect 60 days after that session adjourns, which the game does not yet tell apart.

US-MA.cite: Mass. Const. amend. art. 48, The Referendum, pt. I
US-MA.note: No law takes effect earlier than 90 days after it becomes law, except emergency laws and laws that cannot be the subject of a referendum petition.

US-MD.note: A law takes effect the first day of June after the session that passed it, unless it says otherwise.

US-ME.note: No act takes effect until 90 days after the session's recess; acts take effect on the 91st day (2025: adjourned March 21, effective June 20).

US-MI.note: No act takes effect until 90 days from the end of the session have expired; enrolled 2024 acts read "91st day after final adjournment".

US-MN.note: Ordinary acts take effect the following August 1; acts making appropriations take effect the following July 1, which the game does not yet tell apart.

US-MO.note: A law other than an appropriation act takes effect ninety days after the session adjourns, and the regular session adjourns on May 30, so ordinary laws take effect August 28. Special sessions are not modeled.

US-MP.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the rule the other territories whose rule was read share, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands: an act takes effect when it becomes law.
US-MP.note: Read but not dated: Says only when a bill becomes law; no effective-date rule was found in the constitution or the Commonwealth Code.

US-MS.note: A general law is not enforced until 60 days after its passage unless it says otherwise; the game counts from enactment.

US-MT.note: A statute takes effect on the October 1 after its passage and approval. Appropriations take effect July 1, motor vehicle taxes and fees January 1, and special-session statutes on approval, which the game does not yet tell apart.

US-NC.note: Acts are in force "from and after 60 days after the adjournment of the session"; the game uses the sixtieth day, inferred from the text, not a counted year. Most acts name their own date.

US-ND.note: A law takes effect on the August 1 after it is filed with the secretary of state, or 90 days after filing if filed from August 1 through December 31; the game counts from enactment. Appropriation and tax-rate measures take effect July 1 and emergency measures on filing.

US-NE.note: No act takes effect until three calendar months after the session adjourns; acts take effect the next day (2025: adjourned June 2, effective September 3).

US-NH.note: A law that sets no date takes effect 60 days after passage, not counting the day the governor signs or the legislature last acts; the game counts from enactment.

US-NJ.note: A public act takes effect on the July 4 after its passage unless it says otherwise; the game counts from enactment.

US-NM.note: Laws go into effect ninety days after the session adjourns (2025: adjourned March 22, effective June 20).

US-NV.note: A law takes effect on the October 1 after its passage unless it names another date; the game counts from enactment.

US-NY.note: A law takes effect on the twentieth day after it becomes law unless it names another time.

US-OH.note: A law takes effect ninety days after the governor files it with the secretary of state, the window for a referendum petition; the game counts from enactment. Tax levies, current-expense appropriations and emergency laws take effect at once, which the game does not yet tell apart.

US-OK.note: No act takes effect until ninety days after the session adjourns; the game uses the ninetieth day, inferred from the text, not a counted year. Most acts name November 1 or carry an emergency clause.

US-OR.note: An act takes effect on January 1 of the year after its passage; the game counts from enactment. Emergency clauses are not modeled.

US-PA.note: A statute with no date takes effect 60 days after final enactment. Appropriation acts (§ 1702) and acts affecting local budgets (§ 1703) are dated differently, which the game does not yet tell apart.

US-PR.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the rule the other territories whose rule was read share, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands: an act takes effect when it becomes law.
US-PR.cite: Código Civil de Puerto Rico de 2020, art. 8 (31 L.P.R.A. § 5322)
US-PR.note: Read but not dated: Thirty days after publication, a date the game does not record.

US-RI.note: A statute enacted on or before July 1 takes effect that July 1; one enacted after July 1 takes effect on passage. Subsection (b) delays some acts that raise local costs, which the game does not model.

US-SC.note: An act takes effect on the twentieth day after the governor approves it unless it names another day.

US-SD.note: A regular-session act takes effect on the July 1 after its passage. Special-session acts take effect the 91st day after adjournment, and a referendum petition can suspend an act; neither is modeled.

US-TN.note: A general law takes effect 40 days after passage unless it or its caption says the public welfare requires sooner, as most Tennessee acts do; the game counts from enactment.

US-TX.note: No law takes effect until ninety days after the session adjourns; acts without a date take effect on the 91st day (2025: adjourned June 2, effective September 1), a count inferred from common practice, not read in a statute.

US-UT.note: No act takes effect until sixty days after the session adjourns; acts take effect on the 61st day (2025: adjourned March 7, effective May 7).

US-VA.note: Regular-session laws take effect on the July 1 after the session adjourns. General appropriation laws, special-session laws (the first day of the fourth month after adjournment) and emergency laws are not modeled.

US-VI.note: A bill takes effect on the governor's approval, or on the date it becomes law without approval, unless it says otherwise.

US-VT.note: Laws take effect on the July 1 after their passage unless they say otherwise; many Vermont acts take effect on passage by their own terms.

US-WA.note: No act subject to referendum takes effect until ninety days after the session adjourns; acts take effect on the 91st day (2026: adjourned March 12, effective June 11).

US-WI.note: An act takes effect the day after its date of publication, and the date of publication is the day after enactment.

US-WV.note: An act takes effect 90 days after its passage unless two-thirds of each house direct otherwise; the game counts from enactment.

US-WY.note: Every law takes effect ninety days after the session adjourns unless it names another date; the game uses the ninetieth day, inferred from the text. Most acts name July 1.

US-AL.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the place's law sets no calendar limit on its session, so the session ends on the median last day of the places whose limit was read, for the same year.
US-AL.note: Its rule was not read in days after a session, so its session end was not read either.

US-AR.note: A regular session in odd years opens on the second Monday in January and may not exceed 60 calendar days unless two-thirds extend it; real sessions usually run longer (2023 ended May 1). The even-year fiscal session is limited to 30 days; the constitution opens it in February, but the legislature has moved it to April by law (2024 opened April 10, 2026 April 8), which is the date used.

2026.quote: The Fiscal Session of the 95th General Assembly convened on Wednesday, April 8, 2026 and adjourned sine die on Wednesday, April 29, 2026.

US-AS.cite: Rev. Const. of American Samoa art. II, § 8
US-AS.note: Two regular sessions a year, opening on the second Monday in January and in July, each to last 45 days. Whether those are calendar days was not read; the game counts calendar days.

US-AZ.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the place's law sets no calendar limit on its session, so the session ends on the median last day of the places whose limit was read, for the same year.
US-AZ.note: Sets only the opening day; no limit on length (2025 ran 169 days).

US-DC.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the place's law sets no calendar limit on its session, so the session ends on the median last day of the places whose limit was read, for the same year.
US-DC.note: The Council meets year-round; this date only anchors the estimated rule.

US-FL.note: The session opens on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in March in odd years and the second Tuesday after the first Monday in January in even years, and may not exceed 60 consecutive days unless three-fifths extend it.

2026.quote: On motion by Senator Passidomo, the Senate adjourned sine die at 3:14 p.m.

US-HI.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the place's law sets no calendar limit on its session, so the session ends on the median last day of the places whose limit was read, for the same year.
US-HI.note: Its rule was not read in days after a session, so its session end was not read either.

2026.quote: INFORMING THE HOUSE AND GOVERNOR THAT THE SENATE IS READY TO ADJOURN SINE DIE.

US-ID.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the place's law sets no calendar limit on its session, so the session ends on the median last day of the places whose limit was read, for the same year.
US-ID.note: Sets only the opening day; no limit on length was found.

US-KS.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the place's law sets no calendar limit on its session, so the session ends on the median last day of the places whose limit was read, for the same year.
US-KS.note: Its rule was not read in days after a session, so its session end was not read either.

2026.quote: The Legislature having adjourned sine die on April 10, 2026

US-KY.note: Even-year sessions adjourn by April 15 and odd-year sessions by March 30, the same limit Kentucky's legislative rule pack holds.

US-ME.cite: 3 M.R.S. § 2 (required by Me. Const. art. IV, pt. 3, § 1)
US-ME.note: The first regular session adjourns no later than the third Wednesday in June and the second no later than the third Wednesday in April; two-thirds may extend either.

2026.quote: The Second Regular Session of the 132nd Legislature adjourned SINE DIE on Wednesday, April 29, 2026 at 8:32 PM.

US-MI.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the place's law sets no calendar limit on its session, so the session ends on the median last day of the places whose limit was read, for the same year.
US-MI.note: The session adjourns on a day set by concurrent resolution; its sessions customarily run into December, later than this estimate.

US-MO.note: The regular session adjourns on May 30 each year.

US-NC.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the place's law sets no calendar limit on its session, so the session ends on the median last day of the places whose limit was read, for the same year.
US-NC.note: The session adjourns by resolution; no end date or limit on length.

US-NE.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the place's law sets no calendar limit on its session, so the session ends on the median last day of the places whose limit was read, for the same year.
US-NE.note: The limit is 90 legislative days in odd years and 60 in even years, which are not calendar days (2025 adjourned June 2).

2026.quote: Senator Hansen moved that the One Hundred Ninth Legislature, Second Session, 2026 Session of the Nebraska Legislature, having finished all business before it, now at 2:57 p.m., adjourn sine die.

US-NM.note: The session opens on the third Tuesday in January and may not exceed 60 days in odd years and 30 in even years; it ends at noon on that day (2025: January 21 to March 22).

US-OK.note: The session adjourns sine die no later than 5 p.m. on the last Friday in May.

2026.quote: Pursuant to the Howard declaration, the Senate adjourned sine die at 4:15 p.m.

US-TX.cite: Tex. Const. art. III, § 24(b); Tex. Gov't Code § 301.001
US-TX.note: The regular session opens on the second Tuesday in January of odd years and may not exceed 140 days (2025: January 14 to June 2). Even years hold no regular session.

US-UT.cite: Utah Const. art. VI, § 16(1); Utah Code § 36-3-201
US-UT.note: The session opens on the first Tuesday after the third Monday in January and may not exceed 45 calendar days, not counting holidays; Presidents' Day always falls inside it, so the last day is 45 days after the first (2025: January 21 to March 7).

US-WA.note: The session opens on the second Monday in January and may not exceed 105 consecutive days in odd years and 60 in even years (2026: January 12 to March 12).

2026.quote: The 2026 Regular Session adjourned sine die on March 12

US-WY.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the place's law sets no calendar limit on its session, so the session ends on the median last day of the places whose limit was read, for the same year.
US-WY.note: The limit is 40 legislative working days a year, which are not calendar days.

2026.quote: The Wyoming Legislature concluded the 2026 Budget Session and adjourned sine die on Wednesday at the State Capitol in Cheyenne

us-policy-positions:health-human-service.source: KFF, Status of State Medicaid Expansion Decisions (2026): 41 including D.C. adopted, 10 have not.
us-policy-positions:health-human-service.note: Places first left out were read on 9/29/2026; any still unread take the most common answer among similar places, marked ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE.

US-AS.note: American Samoa runs Medicaid under a waiver that pays for care in proportion to residents under 200 percent of the poverty level with no individual enrollment, so it has not expanded to the adult group (MACPAC, February 2021).

US-GA.note: Pathways covers some adults with a work requirement; not the expansion.

US-GU.note: Guam covers the ACA new adult group up to 133 percent of the local poverty level, per MACPAC's February 2021 territories fact sheet (no later change was found).

US-MP.note: The Northern Mariana Islands set Medicaid eligibility using SSI income and asset standards under a waiver and did not expand to the ACA adult group (MACPAC, February 2021).

US-PR.note: Puerto Rico covers the ACA new adult group up to 133 percent of the local poverty level, per MACPAC's February 2021 territories fact sheet (no later change was found).

US-VI.note: The U.S. Virgin Islands covers the ACA new adult group up to 133 percent of the local poverty level, per MACPAC's February 2021 territories fact sheet (no later change was found).

US-WI.note: Covers adults to 100% of poverty without adopting the expansion.

us-policy-positions:justice-public-safet.source: Permitless (constitutional) carry state lists, January 2026: 29 states; none added or repealed in 2025 or 2026.

US-AS.note: American Samoa makes it a felony to carry a firearm concealed on the person, with exemptions only for officers, prison staff and soldiers, and it separately requires an arms license, so there is no permitless carry.

US-GU.note: Guam law forbids carrying a concealed firearm without a license from the Guam Police Department (a shall-issue license under 10 GCA § 60109.1), and it has no permitless-carry law.

US-MP.note: Commonwealth law bars carrying any firearm in public except in listed cases (home, range, hunting, lawful transport in a locked case) and defines a concealed firearm, so there is no permitless concealed carry.

US-VI.note: The V.I. Supreme Court in Heath v. People (2024) upheld convictions under 14 V.I.C. § 2253(a) for possessing firearms without a license, and the VIPD Firearms License Division still requires a license, so there is no permitless carry.

US-GU.note: The Guam landlord-tenant act sets deposits, notices and remedies but contains no rent limit or rent-increase cap, so Guam has no rent stabilization.

US-HI.cite: Haw. Rev. Stat. ch. 521 (Residential Landlord-Tenant Code)
US-HI.note: The state consumer-protection handbook says there is no limit on the amount of a rent increase because there is no rent control in Hawaii, and no statute barring county rent control was found.

US-IL.note: Enacted 1997; repeal bills (e.g., SB 1260, 2025) have not passed.

US-KY.note: Only the General Assembly may enact rent control on private property.

US-LA.note: Lessor rights may not be altered except by state law (Acts 1977, No. 655); it is an implied rather than rent-specific preemption.

US-MA.cite: Mass. G.L. c. 40P (Rent Control Prohibition Act, 1994 Question 9)
US-MA.note: The Supreme Judicial Court removed a 2026 rent-control initiative from the ballot.

US-MD.cite: Montgomery County rent stabilization law (county ordinance, 2023)
US-MD.note: Maryland has no statewide cap, and Montgomery County runs an Office of Rent Stabilization that limits increases on licensed rental units at least 23 years old.

US-ME.cite: Portland, Me., rent control ordinance (November 2020 referendum)
US-ME.note: Maine has no statewide cap, and Portland voters adopted a local ordinance that limits annual rent increases.

US-MN.note: Local rent control is prohibited unless voters approve it at a general election, which St. Paul and Minneapolis have done, so cities may act only by referendum.

US-MO.note: Preemption was broadened in August 2025 to other landlord-tenant topics.

US-MP.note: The Commonwealth Code has no rent limit or rent-increase cap and does not bar local rent rules, so the Northern Mariana Islands has no statewide rent stabilization.

US-MS.note: Municipalities may not regulate residential rent without prior legislative approval.

US-MT.note: Express denial of local rent-control power added in 2023 (sources name SB 105 or HB 463); opponents said it was already prohibited.

US-NE.note: Signed 2025-04-07; takes effect three months after the 2025 session adjourned (operative date computed, not stated in results).

US-NH.cite: N.H. RSA 31:39; RSA 47:17 (enumerated bylaw powers; no grant over rents); RSA 540, 540-A (no rent-limit provision)
US-NH.note: Weak: no statute bars local rent limits, but New Hampshire follows Dillon's Rule and no statute gives towns or cities power over rents.

US-NJ.cite: N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5 (30-year new-construction exemption); municipal police power (Helmsley v. Borough of Fort Lee, 78 N.J. 200 (1978))
US-NJ.note: The state Department of Community Affairs says New Jersey has no state law controlling rents and municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances, with new construction exempt for 30 years.

US-NM.note: A 2025 repeal bill (SB 216) failed.

US-NV.cite: Nev. Rev. Stat. ch. 118A (NRS 118A.300 notice of rent increase)
US-NV.note: Nevada's landlord-tenant chapter requires only 60 days' notice of a rent increase and contains no bar on local rent control.

US-NY.cite: Emergency Tenant Protection Act of 1974 (local opt-in)
US-NY.note: The state ETPA lets a municipality adopt rent stabilization after declaring a local housing emergency, so limits apply only in New York City and opt-in localities.

US-OH.note: HB 430 added an express preemption of local rent control and rent stabilization.

US-OK.note: Enacted 1988.

US-OR.note: Cap is 7% plus CPI; SB 611 (effective 2023-07-06) added a 10% ceiling; units under 15 years old are exempt; ORS 91.225 still preempts local rent control.

US-PA.note: Weak: no statute bans rent control, but the home-rule law and Dillon's Rule keep cities from capping rents.

US-PR.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the most common answer among the 2 territories read for this question (2 answer no), because this place's own law could not be read.
US-PR.note: Tried: P.R. Laws Ann. tit. 17 rent-regulation statute (Ley de Alquileres Razonables, Ley 464 of 1946) not located: LexJuris yearly law menus 1990-2026 list no rent-control law or repeal (lexjuris.com/lexlex/Leyes<year>/lexl<year>Menu.htm); Ley 132-2011 (repeal of Ley 142-1968) is a building-maintenance law, not rent control; bvirtualogp.pr.gov PDFs 404; the pre-1990 statute text could not be reached.

US-RI.note: Rhode Island requires only 60 days' notice of a rent increase (120 days for month-to-month tenants over 62) and has no statute barring local rent control.

US-TN.note: Enacted 1996; last amended effective 2024-07-01.

US-TX.note: Cities may impose rent control only in a disaster-declared housing emergency with the governor's approval.

US-UT.note: Local rent control requires express legislative approval.

US-VA.cite: Va. Code § 55.1-1200 et seq. (VRLTA supersession) with Dillon Rule
US-VA.note: No rent-specific preemption statute; localities lack authority because the VRLTA supersedes local landlord-tenant ordinances, and 2026 bills HB 278/SB 355 to authorize local rent regulation were sent to study.

US-VI.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the most common answer among the 2 territories read for this question (2 answer no), because this place's own law could not be read.
US-VI.note: Tried: V.I. Code (Lexis-only): https://www.lexisnexis.com/hottopics/vicode/ (viewer loads, no fetchable section text); https://www.legvi.org/vicode/ (HTTP 522); https://vi.public.law/ (no connection); law.justia.com (blocked); Legislature bill-tracker PDFs (File Not Found).

US-VT.note: Vermont's rental chapter, current through the 2025 session, has no rent cap and no bar on local rent control, though a city would need a charter change approved by the legislature.

US-WA.note: Cap is the lesser of 7% plus CPI or 10% over 12 months (9.683% for 2026); new construction under 15 years exempt; expires 2040-07-01; RCW 35.21.830 still preempts local rent control.

US-WV.note: Cities hold only the powers the code lists, and the list in § 8-12-5 (read 9/28/2026) grants no power over rents; its item (43) is a general welfare clause. The home rule section adds that municipalities "may not prohibit or effectively limit the rental of a property" (§ 8-1-5a(k)). So a typical city may not set rent limits.

US-WY.cite: Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 to -1211 (Residential Rental Property Act)
US-WY.note: No rent-control preemption appears in Wyoming's landlord-tenant, municipal (Title 15) or property (Title 34) statutes as compiled in May 2026, so the claim of a preemption statute is unsupported.

us-policy-positions:education.universal-.source: Education Commission of the States and NIEER (2025): Colorado, Florida, Oklahoma, Vermont and D.C. offer universal pre-K to four-year-olds.
us-policy-positions:education.universal-.note: Places first left out were read on 9/29/2026; any still unread take the most common answer among similar places, marked ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE.

US-AK.note: The Alaska Pre-Elementary program is a competitive grant to selected school districts, not a place for every child. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-AL.note: First Class Pre-K is a voluntary grant program open to four-year-olds, but it funds limited classrooms rather than a place for every family that asks. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-AR.note: Arkansas Better Chance serves children with income or risk factors listed in the program rules, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-AS.note: The code sets up an early childhood education program in the Department of Education but promises no place to every four-year-old, and it does not bar villages from funding preschool.

US-AZ.note: State support is a Quality First scholarship for lower-income families, not a place for every child. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-CA.note: From the 2025-26 school year every child who turns four by September 1 must be admitted to transitional kindergarten, and the date is the start of that school year.

US-CT.note: School Readiness funds are for children in lower-income households or priority towns, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-DE.note: The Early Childhood Assistance Program serves four-year-olds who qualify for Head Start, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-GA.note: Georgia's Pre-K Program is open to every four-year-old but voluntary for providers and capped by lottery funds, so the state does not guarantee a place for every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-GU.note: Guam's education code starts public schooling at kindergarten (five years old by July 31) and only lets gifted four-year-olds enter early, so it funds no preschool for every child, and it does not bar villages from doing so.

US-HI.note: State preschool seats are limited and the Preschool Open Doors subsidy is income-based, so not every family gets a place. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-IA.note: The Statewide Voluntary Preschool Program is open to every four-year-old resident and funded for each child enrolled, though each school district chooses to take part.

US-ID.note: State law funds no preschool program of its own for four-year-olds, and it does not bar cities or counties from funding one.

US-IL.note: Preschool for All is a competitive grant program aimed at children at risk of academic failure, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-IN.note: On My Way Pre-K is a voucher for low-income four-year-olds, not a place for every child. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-KS.note: State preschool money goes to at-risk children and a small pilot, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-KY.note: State preschool serves four-year-olds under an income limit and children with disabilities, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-LA.note: LA 4 and related programs serve children at or below 200 percent of poverty, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-MA.note: Commonwealth Preschool Partnerships grants go to selected districts, which set their own priorities, so not every family gets a place. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-MD.note: State prekindergarten is free for four-year-olds from lower-income families, with expansion under the Blueprint, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-ME.note: The public preschool program is optional for each school unit and funded only where the unit chooses to run it (20-A M.R.S. § 4271), so no family is assured a place. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-MI.note: The Great Start Readiness Program funds capped grants to intermediate districts, with children served by eligibility and priority guidelines (MCL 388.1632d), not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-MN.note: Voluntary Pre-K and school readiness money serves children with at least one risk factor, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-MO.note: State pre-K counts only a small share of a district's low-income children, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-MP.note: The Education Act tells the Board of Education to provide programs suited to student needs but does not entitle every four-year-old to a preschool place, and it does not bar municipalities from funding preschool.

US-MS.note: Early Learning Collaboratives are grant-funded in selected communities, not a place for every child. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-MT.note: State preschool programs admit children by screening scores at selected sites, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-NC.note: NC Pre-K serves children at or below 75 percent of state median income plus a small share with risk factors, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-ND.note: State-funded preschool is limited grants for low-income children, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-NE.note: State preschool requires that most children in each program have a listed risk factor, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-NH.note: State law funds no preschool program of its own for four-year-olds, and it does not bar cities or counties from funding one.

US-NJ.note: Preschool is funded in Abbott and expansion districts, about half of districts, not statewide for every child. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-NM.note: NM PreK is a competitive grant program with priority for Title I attendance zones, not a place for every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-NV.note: State pre-K goes to programs serving children with the highest need, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-NY.note: Universal Prekindergarten is funded as grants to participating school districts, and the Regents' goal of truly universal access is set for 2035, so no place is assured for every child. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-OH.note: Early Childhood Education grants serve children found eligible through a unified state process, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-OR.note: Oregon Pre-K follows federal Head Start income rules and serves children from low-income families, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-PA.note: Pre-K Counts serves children in households up to 300 percent of poverty through competitive grants, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-PR.cite: Ley 85-2018 (Ley de Reforma Educativa de Puerto Rico)
US-PR.note: The Education Reform Act lists pre-kindergarten among the basic school programs but gives no four-year-old a right to a state-funded place, and it does not bar municipalities from funding preschool.

US-RI.note: State Pre-K is a lottery in participating communities only, not a place for every child. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-SC.note: The Child Early Reading Development and Education Program serves children eligible for free lunch or Medicaid, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-SD.note: State law funds no preschool program of its own for four-year-olds, and it does not bar cities or counties from funding one.

US-TN.note: Voluntary Pre-K gives priority to low-income children and has limited seats, not a place for every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-TX.note: Public prekindergarten is for four-year-olds who meet listed eligibility, such as low income or limited English, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-UT.note: Preschool grants prioritize high-quality seats for eligible three- and four-year-olds, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-VA.note: The Virginia Preschool Initiative serves four-year-olds identified as at risk, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-VI.note: The Department of Education must run a territory-wide voluntary pre-kindergarten program for four-year-olds, aimed at all children who are four, with selection criteria left to Commissioner rules; the section was added March 7, 2012.

US-WA.note: The Early Childhood Education and Assistance Program is for children who meet income or special-circumstance criteria, not every family. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-WI.note: Four-year-old kindergarten is open to every child if a school district offers it, but districts are not required to offer it, so the state does not assure a place for every child. State law does not bar cities or counties from funding preschool.

US-WV.note: County boards must provide early childhood education programs for all children who are four before the school-year cutoff date, open to every child.

US-WY.note: State law funds no preschool program of its own for four-year-olds, and it does not bar cities or counties from funding one.

us-policy-positions:labor-workforce.rais.source: data/research/money/minimum-wage-2026.json (U.S. Department of Labor, July 1, 2026): yes where the state's basic rate is above the federal $7.25.

US-AS.cite: Pub. L. 110-28 § 8103, as amended by Pub. L. 114-61; 29 U.S.C. § 206 note
US-AS.note: American Samoa has no territorial minimum wage; its industry rates are set by federal law and stay below $7.25 (for example $6.20 for retail since September 30, 2024) until they reach the federal rate.

us-policy-positions:fiscal.adopt-income-.source: data/research/money/state-income-tax-2026.json (2026 brackets): the 9 states with no tax on wages answer no.

US-AS.note: American Samoa adopts the federal income-tax rules as the separate Samoan Income Tax, a territorial income tax with withholding on wages.

US-GU.note: The Guam Organic Act applies the federal income-tax laws in Guam as a separate Guam Territorial income tax payable to the government of Guam, so wages are taxed.

US-MP.note: The Commonwealth adopts the Internal Revenue Code as the Northern Marianas Territorial Income Tax, a broad income tax on wages.

US-PR.cite: Ley 1-2011 (Internal Revenue Code for a New Puerto Rico)
US-PR.note: Puerto Rico taxes individual income under its own Internal Revenue Code of 2011, with a graduated schedule reaching 33 percent.

US-VI.note: The federal income tax laws are in force in the Virgin Islands as its own income tax on wages, with the proceeds paid to the territory.

US-AK.note: Section 12.30.011(b) lets the judge require a cash appearance bond, a bail bond with sureties or a cash performance bond; HB 49 (2019) repealed SB 91's release presumptions.

US-AL.note: Rule 7.2 lets the court release on recognizance or an appearance bond and refers to secured appearance bonds; money bail remains a standard condition.

US-AR.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the most common answer among the 49 states and D.C. read for this question (46 answer no), because this place's own law could not be read.
US-AR.note: Tried: Ark. R. Crim. P. 9.2 and Ark. Const. art. 2, sec. 8: arcourts.gov rules pages (404 or script-rendered), sos.arkansas.gov constitution PDF (404), arkleg.state.ar.us constitution PDF (returns a blank GIF), law.justia.com, casetext.com (closed), lawserver.com (script wall).

US-AZ.note: Section 13-3967 lets the judge require a deposit of cash or other security as a release condition.

US-CA.note: Bail is accepted in cash or surety bond under countywide bail schedules; voters rejected SB 10's replacement of cash bail (Proposition 25, November 2020).

US-CO.note: Section 16-4-104 still authorizes a bond with secured monetary conditions, although unsecured personal recognizance bonds come first.

US-CT.note: Practice Book § 38-4 lists 7 percent cash bail and bonds with surety among release conditions and bars judges from prohibiting surety bonds; the statute (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 54-64a) could not be fetched from cga.ct.gov.

US-DC.note: A judge may not set a financial condition that results in detention, so money bail is effectively unused (provision dates from the 1992 amendments). H.R. 5214 (D.C. Cash Bail Reform Act) passed the House on 11/19/2025 but had not passed the Senate, so it was not law on 1/1/2026 (GovTrack, https://www.govtrack.us/congress/bills/119/hr5214).

US-DE.note: Delaware prefers nonmonetary conditions but still authorizes bonds guaranteed by financial terms, including cash-only bonds.

US-FL.note: Florida law sets bail criteria and requires monetary bonds of at least $2,000 in certain failure-to-appear cases.

US-GA.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the most common answer among the 49 states and D.C. read for this question (46 answer no), because this place's own law could not be read.
US-GA.note: Tried: O.C.G.A. 17-6-1 and SB 63 (2025): legis.ga.gov API (HTTP 500 or script-only), georgia.public.law (no connection), lawserver.com (script wall), casetext.com (closed), gov.georgia.gov signed-bill page (not the bill text), ballotpedia.org (HTTP 202 empty).

US-GU.note: Section 40.20(d) authorizes a bond secured by cash, other property or qualified sureties; the compilation is current to 6/24/2021.

US-HI.note: Section 804-9 has judges set a reasonable bail amount considering ability to afford it; money bail remains lawful.

US-IA.note: Section 811.2 authorizes cash deposits and bail bonds with sufficient surety as release conditions.

US-ID.note: The Idaho Bail Act defines bail as a monetary amount required for release and regulates bail agents and bail bonds.

US-IL.note: The Pretrial Fairness Act (SAFE-T Act, P.A. 101-652) abolished monetary bail on 9/18/2023; release is decided by conditions or a detention hearing. The statute page on ilga.gov could not be fetched (TLS failure / egress block), so the source is secondary.

US-IN.note: Rule 2.6 (effective 1/1/2024) favors release without money bail for low-risk arrestees but expressly authorizes money bail by surety bond or cash deposit.

US-KS.note: Section 22-2802 authorizes appearance bonds with sureties and cash bonds.

US-KY.note: Partial: Kentucky bans commercial bail bondsmen and presumes release on unsecured bond for low- and moderate-risk defendants, but courts still set bail and the statute credits jail time toward it.

US-LA.note: Article 321 lists commercial surety, secured personal surety and cash deposit among the types of bail.

US-MA.note: Section 58 presumes personal recognizance but allows cash bail (or an equivalent surety bond) set with regard to financial resources.

US-MD.note: Section 5-205 lets District Court judges set bond or bail, including cash bail; Maryland's 2017 court rule favors nonfinancial conditions but did not abolish money bail.

US-ME.note: Section 1026 lets the judicial officer require a bail bond with sureties or a financial condition, considering ability to pay.

US-MI.note: Section 765.6 has the court fix a bail amount, with 10 percent deposit or surety bonds.

US-MN.note: Rule 6.02 lets the court require an appearance bond, cash deposit or other security when recognizance is not enough.

US-MO.note: Section 544.455 lets the judge require a bail bond with sureties or a cash deposit.

US-MP.note: Rule 46 lets the judge require an appearance bond with a cash deposit or a bail bond with sureties.

US-MS.note: Rule 8 provides for secured appearance bonds and publishes recommended money bond ranges.

US-MT.note: Section 46-9-401 lists cash deposits, real estate pledges and surety bonds as forms of bail.

US-NC.note: Section 15A-534 authorizes secured appearance bonds backed by cash, mortgage or surety.

US-ND.note: Rule 46 lets the magistrate require an appearance bond with a cash deposit or other security.

US-NE.note: Section 29-901 authorizes appearance bonds with a cash deposit of up to 10 percent, or full bail bonds.

US-NH.note: Section 597:2 authorizes cash or corporate surety bail, set considering ability to post it.

US-NJ.note: Partial but near-abolition: the Criminal Justice Reform Act relies primarily on non-monetary release and allows monetary bail only when no other condition will assure appearance; it took effect with the 2014 amendment to N.J. Const. art. I, para. 11 (January 1, 2017).

US-NM.note: Partial: the 2016 amendment (SJR 1) allows felony detention without bail and bars holding someone solely for inability to post a money or property bond, but keeps bail by sufficient sureties.

US-NV.note: Section 178.502 lets the court require sureties or accept cash for a bail bond.

US-NY.note: Partial: since 1/1/2020 money bail is barred for most misdemeanors and nonviolent felonies, but it remains a standard condition for qualifying offenses (list since expanded); nysenate.gov refused the fetch, so the source is secondary.

US-OH.note: Section 2937.22 lists deposits of cash and bonds and surety undertakings as forms of bail.

US-OK.note: The constitution makes all persons bailable by sufficient sureties (with listed exceptions); the statutes (22 O.S. § 1105) could not be fetched from oscn.net or oklegislature.gov.

US-OR.note: Partial: Oregon has no commercial bail bonds, but security release requires depositing 10 percent of a money security amount set by the magistrate.

US-PA.note: Rule 524 lists monetary conditions and full cash bail among the types of release on bail.

US-PR.cite: P.R. Const. art. II, § 11; P.R. R. Crim. P. 218
US-PR.note: The constitution guarantees admission to bail before conviction and bars excessive bail; bail (fianza) is a money amount. Rule 218 itself could not be fetched.

US-RI.note: Section 12-13-1 releases defendants upon recognizance with sufficient surety or sureties.

US-SC.note: Section 17-15-10 lets the court require an appearance bond with good and sufficient sureties.

US-SD.note: Section 23A-43-3 lets the court require an appearance bond backed by a cash or security deposit.

US-TN.note: The constitution makes all prisoners bailable by sufficient sureties; Tennessee's code (Tenn. Code Ann. tit. 40, ch. 11) is not on a fetchable official site.

US-TX.cite: Tex. Code Crim. Proc. ch. 17 (as amended by S.B. 6, 87th Leg., 2d C.S., 2021)
US-TX.note: S.B. 6 (2021) regulates setting bail amounts and restricts release on personal bond for certain defendants, so monetary bail remains standard.

US-UT.note: Section 77-20-205 lists a financial condition among release conditions; the fetched page is the version effective 5/6/2026, and the financial-condition option also existed on 1/1/2026.

US-VA.note: Section 19.2-123 authorizes secure bonds satisfied by sureties or cash.

US-VT.note: Section 7554 lets the judicial officer require a secured appearance bond or surety bond, considering financial means.

US-WA.note: CrR 3.2 lets the court require a bond with a cash or security deposit or a surety bond.

US-WI.note: Partial: Wisconsin bars commercial bail bonds, but judges may require bail bonds with sureties or cash deposits.

US-WV.note: Article 1C governs admission to bail and review of the amount of bail; money bail remains lawful.

US-WY.note: Title 7, ch. 10 governs bail amounts, sureties and forfeiture of bail (details in W.R.Cr.P. 46.1).

us-policy-positions:government-operation.source: NCSL Voter ID Laws (updated 07/02/2025) and ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id; Ballotpedia voter ID pages and 10/2025 amendment roundup; state statutes and election offices (Ohio R.C. 3505.18, N.C.G.S. 163-166.16, W.Va. HB 3016, N.H. HB 1569, Neb. LB 514, Ky. SB 2); law in force 01/01/2026.
us-policy-positions:government-operation.note: Places first left out were read on 9/29/2026; any still unread take the most common answer among similar places, marked ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE.

US-AK.note: Non-strict non-photo ID.

US-AL.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without photo ID may vote a regular ballot if two poll workers identify the voter.

US-AR.note: Strict photo: Act 249 of 2021 removed the affidavit fail-safe, so a voter without photo ID votes provisionally and must show ID by noon the Monday after the election.

US-AS.note: At the polls a voter signs the poll book and gives identification only if a district official asks, with no photo requirement (photo ID is required once, when registering).

US-AZ.note: Strict non-photo: photo ID or two non-photo documents with name and address.

US-CA.note: No document required at the polls (first-time voters under federal law excepted).

US-CO.note: Non-photo ID accepted; 2025 SB 1 added more non-photo IDs.

US-CT.note: Non-strict non-photo ID; a voter may sign an affidavit.

US-DC.note: No document required at the polls.

US-DE.note: Non-strict non-photo ID; a voter may sign an affidavit.

US-FL.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without photo ID casts a provisional ballot that counts if the signature matches the registration record.

US-GA.note: Strict photo; 2025 HB 296 requires a driver's license used for voting to be a physical card.

US-GU.note: The Guam Election Commission states voters must present a photo ID issued by a federal, state, Guam school or government of Guam entity to vote; the exact 3 GCA section was not confirmed.

US-HI.note: Act 136 of 2019 repealed the rule that voters show ID on request; no ID is required except as federal law requires.

US-IA.note: Non-strict non-photo: the non-photo Iowa voter ID card is accepted.

US-ID.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without ID may sign an affidavit and vote; 2023 HB 124 removed student IDs, and 2026 SB 1322 (effective 07/01/2026) adds verification data to the affidavit.

US-IL.note: No document required at the polls.

US-IN.note: Strict photo.

US-KS.note: Strict photo.

US-KY.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without photo ID may sign a reasonable impediment declaration and show a secondary ID; SB 154 later narrows the accepted secondary IDs starting in 2026.

US-LA.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without photo ID may sign an affidavit and vote a regular ballot.

US-MA.note: No document required at the polls.

US-MD.note: No document required at the polls.

US-ME.note: No document required at the polls; a voter ID ballot question failed in November 2025.

US-MI.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without photo ID may sign an affidavit and vote a regular ballot.

US-MN.note: No document required at the polls.

US-MO.note: Non-strict photo in part: 2022 HB 1878 removed non-photo alternatives; a voter without photo ID votes provisionally, and the ballot counts if the signature matches or the voter returns with ID.

US-MP.note: The Commonwealth Election Commission pamphlet says a pictured ID is required to be issued a ballot at the polls; the statute located covers early voting.

US-MS.note: Strict photo.

US-MT.note: Non-strict non-photo: a utility bill or other document with name and address is accepted; the 2024 Montana Supreme Court ruling kept student IDs.

US-NC.note: Photo ID in force since the 2023 municipal elections; a voter without one may sign a reasonable impediment declaration and cast a provisional ballot that counts unless the declaration is found false.

US-ND.note: Strict non-photo: ID must show a residential address but need not bear a photo.

US-NE.note: Strict photo with a reasonable impediment certification for voters who cannot obtain ID. Signed 6/1/2023 (LB 514); first applied at the 5/14/2024 primary.

US-NH.note: Photo ID has been asked for years; HB 1569 made it strict by removing the ID affidavit effective 11/11/2024, and HB 323 drops student IDs effective 06/02/2026.

US-NJ.note: No document required at the polls.

US-NM.note: No document required at the polls; a voter may state identifying information verbally.

US-NV.note: No document required; AB 499 (photo ID) was vetoed on 06/12/2025, and a photo ID constitutional amendment faces its second vote in November 2026.

US-NY.note: No document required at the polls.

US-OH.note: Strict photo under HB 458; a voter without photo ID votes provisionally and must show ID within four days.

US-OK.note: Non-strict non-photo: the non-photo voter identification card is accepted.

US-OR.note: All-mail voting; no document required.

US-PA.note: No document required except for first-time voters at a polling place.

US-PR.cite: P.R. Laws tit. 16, § 4573 (Código Electoral de 2020)
US-PR.note: The 2020 Electoral Code names the photo electoral ID card or other listed photo IDs as the identification valid for voting; the fallback for a voter with none was not confirmed.

US-RI.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without photo ID casts a provisional ballot that counts if the signature matches.

US-SC.note: Non-strict photo: a voter with a reasonable impediment may sign an affidavit, show the non-photo registration card and vote provisionally.

US-SD.note: Non-strict photo: a voter without photo ID may sign an affidavit and vote a regular ballot.

US-TN.note: Strict photo.

US-TX.note: Non-strict photo: a voter who cannot reasonably obtain photo ID may sign a reasonable impediment declaration and show a supporting document.

US-UT.note: Non-photo documents accepted in person; 2025 HB 300 changes mail-ballot ID, not the in-person photo question.

US-VA.note: Non-strict non-photo since the 2020 repeal of photo ID.

US-VI.note: The Election System says a voter gives an election officer identification at the polls but, without proper identification, signs an affidavit and votes, and it names no photo requirement.

US-VT.note: No document required at the polls.

US-WA.note: A voting-center voter may either provide ID or sign a ballot declaration, so no document is required.

US-WI.cite: Wis. Stat. § 6.79(2); Wis. Const. art. III, § 1
US-WI.note: Strict photo; voters constitutionalized the requirement in April 2025.

US-WV.note: Non-strict photo: HB 3016 replaced non-photo ID with photo ID effective 07/11/2025; a poll worker who has known the voter for six months may vouch, and others vote provisionally after an affidavit.

US-WY.note: Strict non-photo per NCSL: the 2021 law (HB 75) mostly lists photo IDs but also accepts Medicare and Medicaid cards.

US-AK.note: Approved by 2016 ballot measure (Measure 1); eligible Permanent Fund Dividend applicants are registered with a mailed opt-out notice (back-end), in operation since 2017.

US-AL.note: Not among the states NCSL lists with automatic voter registration; registration is by the person's own application, including the ordinary motor-voter offer.

US-AR.note: Not among the states NCSL lists with automatic voter registration; registration is by the person's own application, including the ordinary motor-voter offer.

US-AS.note: A person is registered only by appearing before an election officer with government photo identification and signing a sworn application, with no automatic registration.

US-AZ.note: Not among the states NCSL lists with automatic voter registration; registration is by the person's own application, including the ordinary motor-voter offer.

US-CA.note: California New Motor Voter Program, enacted 2015 and in operation at the DMV since 2018.

US-CO.note: Front-end AVR at the DMV from 2017, converted to back-end AVR (mailed opt-out) in 2020.

US-CT.note: Administrative DMV system from 2016, codified and expanded to other agencies by 2021 law; applicants must decline at the transaction (front-end, hard-stop design).

US-DC.note: Automatic Voter Registration Amendment Act passed by the Council on 11/01/2016; implemented at the DMV.

US-DE.note: Enacted 2021 (back-end at the DMV); in operation from 06/21/2023 for voters not already registered.

US-FL.note: Not among the states NCSL lists with automatic voter registration; registration is by the person's own application, including the ordinary motor-voter offer.

US-GA.note: Adopted administratively (opt-out at the Department of Driver Services) in fall 2016, not by a separate AVR statute.

US-GU.note: A Guam voter is registered only by the person's own sworn affidavit or online application with proof of citizenship, with no automatic registration through an agency.

US-HI.note: Hawaii's 2021 'automatic registration' law registers a license applicant only if the applicant chooses to register on the form (mandatory choice, not opt-out); a 2026 bill (HB 2132) proposed expanding it.

US-IA.note: Not among the states NCSL lists with automatic voter registration; registration is by the person's own application, including the ordinary motor-voter offer.

US-ID.note: Not among AVR states; registration is by the person's own application (Idaho is exempt from the NVRA's motor-voter requirement).

US-IL.note: Signed 08/2017 (unanimous legislature); implemented at the Secretary of State driver facilities and other agencies from 2018.

US-IN.note: Not among the states NCSL lists with automatic voter registration; registration is by the person's own application, including the ordinary motor-voter offer.

US-KS.note: Not among the states NCSL lists with automatic voter registration; registration is by the person's own application, including the ordinary motor-voter offer.
