US-AK.note: Alaska's police protection chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city or borough may set one up under its own powers.

US-AL.note: Alabama's peace officer standards law says nothing for or against a civilian complaint board, and Birmingham created its own civilian review board by city action in 2021.

US-AR.note: Arkansas's municipal police officers' bill of rights neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city may set one up under its own powers.

US-AS.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the most common answer among the 4 territories read for this question (3 answer no), because this place's own law could not be read.
US-AS.note: Tried: Read A.S.C.A. 46.0201 at https://asbar.org/code-annotated/46-0201-appointment-of-officers/ (police appointments) but the asbar.org section index could not be browsed to check the rest of title 46 and the public safety department chapter for a civilian board, and a search found no civilian complaint board for American Samoa; no second official copy (osas.as administrative code pdf) was read.

US-AZ.note: At least two-thirds of any government body that investigates officer misconduct or recommends or imposes discipline must be certified officers from the officer's own department, so a civilian board may only review decisions after the fact.

US-CA.note: Counties may create civilian sheriff oversight boards and an inspector general with subpoena power over the sheriff's department; AB 1185 took effect in 2021 and AB 847 (ch. 383) amended the section effective 1/1/2026.

US-CO.note: Colorado's 2020 police integrity act sets duties for agencies and the state POST board but neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city or county may set one up under its own powers, as Denver did.

US-CT.cite: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 7-294aaa (P.A. 20-1, July Special Session)
US-CT.note: A town may by ordinance set up a civilian police review board and may give it power to issue subpoenas and to compel documents; the section refers to boards existing before July 31, 2020, the date the act was signed.

US-DC.note: The District's Office of Police Complaints and Police Complaints Board receive, investigate and adjudicate civilian complaints against Metropolitan Police officers.

US-DE.note: Delaware's police officers' due process chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian board, and a 2022 bill to authorize community oversight boards dropped that provision; Wilmington's complaint board rests on a city ordinance.

US-FL.cite: Fla. Stat. § 112.533(3) (ch. 2024-86, Laws of Fla., HB 601)
US-FL.note: Since 7/1/2024 local governments may not adopt ordinances on investigating police misconduct complaints or on civilian oversight of those investigations; sheriffs and police chiefs may set up civilian boards that only review policies.

US-GA.note: No Georgia statute creates or bars a civilian police board, and the Atlanta Citizen Review Board works under a city ordinance that gives it subpoena power.

US-GU.note: Guam's Community Police Review Commission, first created in 1999 and re-established by Public Law 30-076 on 1/22/2010, receives complaints against Guam Police Department employees, investigates them, holds hearings and may issue subpoenas.

US-HI.note: Chapter 139 created a statewide Law Enforcement Standards Board with a majority of public members (four public and two officers) to certify officers and act on misconduct, though the board was still being staffed in 2026.

US-IA.note: A city with a civil service commission may not adopt or enforce an ordinance or any other measure that creates a board for citizen review of police officers, which ended the boards in Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and other cities.

US-ID.note: Idaho's peace officer standards chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city or county may set one up under its own powers.

US-IL.note: Illinois's Uniform Peace Officers' Disciplinary Act neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, and Chicago's civilian office and community commission rest on city ordinances.

US-IN.note: Indiana's police merit system chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, though a merit board keeps final say over discipline, so a city may set up only an advisory board.

US-KS.note: Kansas's peace officer standards article neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city or county may set one up under its own powers.

US-KY.note: No state law requires civilian oversight, and none bars a local board: § 15.520(5) sends a complaint to a law enforcement agency for investigation, and Louisville Metro runs its own civilian review board (Build 3 review, 9/29/2026).

US-LA.note: Louisiana's law enforcement officers' rights chapter sets minimum steps for an investigation but neither creates nor bars a civilian board, and New Orleans' independent police monitor rests on its city charter.

US-MA.note: The Peace Officer Standards and Training Commission, a nine-member board with a civilian majority, has a division of police standards that receives every agency's complaints, investigates officer misconduct and recommends discipline up to decertification.

US-MD.cite: Md. Code, Pub. Safety §§ 3-102, 3-104 (Police Accountability Act of 2021)
US-MD.note: Every county must have a police accountability board that takes public complaints and an administrative charging committee with civilian members that reviews each misconduct investigation, can require more investigation and subpoenas, and decides whether to charge the officer.

US-ME.note: Maine's only statewide complaint body is a committee of the Criminal Justice Academy board that has just two citizen members out of five and investigates certified officers for certification, and no Maine statute creates, requires or bars a local civilian board.

US-MI.note: Michigan's law enforcement standards act neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, and Detroit's civilian police commission, with subpoena power, rests on the city charter.

US-MN.note: Local governments may create civilian oversight councils that investigate misconduct after any criminal case, subpoena testimony and documents, and make findings and recommend discipline to the chief.

US-MO.note: Since 2000 cities and counties may create civilian review boards to receive, investigate and make findings on public complaints; a 2024 amendment (SB 754, effective 8/28/2024) limits them to those powers and voids any broader authority.

US-MP.note: The Northern Mariana Islands' public safety department chapter creates no civilian complaint board and nothing in it bars one.

US-MS.note: Mississippi's law enforcement training chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city may set one up under its own powers.

US-MT.note: Montana's peace officer standards provisions neither create nor bar a civilian complaint board, so a city or county may set one up under its own powers.

US-NC.note: No state law requires civilian oversight or bars a local board; confidential personnel files and local acts (Charlotte, S.B. 193 of 2021) limit what a board may see and do, and Charlotte, Durham and Raleigh run their own boards (Build 3 review, 9/29/2026).

US-ND.note: North Dakota's peace officer standards chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city may set one up under its own powers.

US-NE.note: Nebraska's police standards statutes neither create nor bar a civilian complaint board, so a city may set one up under its own powers.

US-NH.note: The state Conduct Review Committee has four law enforcement members and three public members and reviews misconduct allegations for certification, and no New Hampshire statute creates, requires or bars a local civilian board.

US-NJ.cite: N.J.S.A. 40A:14-118; Fraternal Order of Police, Newark Lodge No. 12 v. City of Newark, 244 N.J. 75 (2020)
US-NJ.note: In 2020 the New Jersey Supreme Court held that a city may not give its civilian review board subpoena power or a role in discipline, because state law leaves those to the police department and the Attorney General's rules, so boards can only advise.

US-NM.note: New Mexico's law enforcement training article neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, and Albuquerque's civilian oversight agency rests on a city ordinance.

US-NV.note: Cities and counties may create civilian review boards whose panels review internal investigations, recommend discipline and may subpoena witnesses and documents; they have no jurisdiction over alleged crimes.

US-NY.note: Executive Law section 75 (June 2020) created the Law Enforcement Misconduct Investigative Office, an independent statewide office that receives and investigates complaints of excessive force and other misconduct by officers in more than 500 local agencies.

US-OH.note: Ohio's municipal police chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, and Cleveland and Columbus run boards under their own charters.

US-OK.note: No Oklahoma statute creates or bars a civilian police board, and Oklahoma City has one while Tulsa's council took up an oversight ordinance on its own authority.

US-OR.note: Oregon's police records statute names civilian or community oversight boards designated by a city or agency as bodies that investigate allegations of officer misconduct, so state law recognizes local boards and does not limit them.

US-PA.note: No Pennsylvania statute creates or bars civilian police review; Pittsburgh's board, with subpoena power, comes from its home rule charter, though the Commonwealth Court held in 2011 that a state criminal history records law limits which police records it may compel.

US-PR.cite: P.R. Laws Ann. tit. 25, § 3531 et seq. (Ley 20-2017, cap. 2)
US-PR.note: Puerto Rico's police law creates no civilian complaint board and does not bar one, and it placed the police bureau under the Secretary of Public Safety (Law 83-2025 later made it a separate agency).

US-RI.note: The Law Enforcement Officers' Due Process, Accountability, and Transparency Act sets how a law enforcement agency investigates officers and says nothing for or against a civilian board, so Providence's review board rests on its own city law.

US-SC.note: South Carolina's law enforcement training chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city may set one up under its own powers.

US-SD.note: South Dakota's law enforcement standards provisions neither create nor bar a civilian complaint board, so a city or county may set one up under its own powers.

US-TN.cite: Tenn. Code Ann. Title 38, Ch. 8 (Pub. Ch. 454, 2023, SB 591)
US-TN.note: The 2023 law abolished community oversight boards and lets cities create police advisory and review committees that send complaints to internal affairs, review its files and may only ask for further investigation; they have no subpoena power.

US-TX.note: Texas law recognizes municipal civilian oversight boards and sets who may serve on one (S.B. 1957, effective 6/20/2025) but neither gives such a board investigative power nor bars a city from creating one.

US-UT.note: A city may not create a board with power independent of the police chief to overrule hiring, veto policy or approve the budget, but the law lets a city appoint an oversight board and does not stop one from reviewing complaints, so state law neither creates nor bars a complaint-review board.

US-VA.note: Localities may create civilian oversight bodies that investigate complaints, issue findings, make binding discipline decisions in serious cases and seek court subpoenas (2020 Special Session I, cc. 29-30).

US-VI.note: The Virgin Islands Police Department chapter creates no civilian complaint board and nothing in it bars one, and the territory has no local governments that could create their own.

US-VT.note: The Vermont Criminal Justice Council takes and adjudicates complaints of officer misconduct for certification but is mostly law enforcement and government members with seven public members, and no Vermont statute creates, requires or bars a local civilian board.

US-WA.note: The 2021 law created the Office of Independent Investigations in the governor's office to investigate police uses of deadly force independently of police agencies; it covers serious incidents, not every complaint.

US-WI.note: State law gives each city's citizen police and fire commission the power to hear charges filed by any aggrieved person against an officer and to impose discipline; it is a hearing board rather than an investigating office.

US-WV.note: West Virginia's law enforcement standards article neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city may set one up under its own powers.

US-WY.note: Wyoming's peace officer standards article neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city or county may set one up under its own powers.

us-policy-positions:government-operation.source: State legislature code and constitution pages fetched 2026-09-28 (current text in force on 2026-01-01), plus a few secondary sources where legislature hosts refused: municipal league pages (IML, Arkansas Municipal League, MTAS), state encyclopedias (Alabama, Georgia), the Colorado Legislative Council brief (May 2020), Wikisource copies of the CT, KS, NY and CNMI constitutions, and Wikipedia's 'Home rule in the United States' table (IN and NM only).
us-policy-positions:government-operation.note: Places first left out were read on 9/29/2026; any still unread take the most common answer among similar places, marked ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE.

US-AK.note: Home-rule boroughs and cities may exercise all legislative powers not prohibited by law or charter, and the constitution orders liberal construction of every local government's powers.

US-AL.note: Cities and towns hold only the powers the legislature delegates to them, and counties have no general grant at all, so Dillon's Rule governs.

US-AR.note: Act 1187 of 2011 gave every municipality full legislative power over municipal affairs and declared Dillon's Rule inapplicable; before that, only first-class cities had it. Section 14-43-601 lists the matters reserved as state affairs.

US-AS.note: Village councils may make regulations only on matters of a strictly local nature, they take effect only after the Department of Samoan Affairs approves them, and penalties are capped at $25, so local power is narrow and delegated.

US-AZ.note: Only charter cities (population over 3,500, including Phoenix and Tucson) hold home rule, and their charters prevail over conflicting laws on city matters; the general-law cities, which are most cities by count, have only statutory powers.

US-CA.note: Every county and city may make any local police, sanitary and other regulations that do not conflict with general laws, and charter cities also control their municipal affairs.

US-CO.note: The 103 home-rule municipalities, including Denver, may legislate on local matters, but statutory towns remain strictly subject to state law.

US-CT.note: The General Assembly delegates only the legislative authority it chooses to towns, cities and boroughs, and the Home Rule Act lets them choose their charter structure but not residual powers. The source is a Wikisource copy because cga.ct.gov refused connections.

US-DC.note: The District has no municipalities, and its own legislative power extends to all rightful subjects of legislation, subject to the Home Rule Act's limits and Congress's reserved power to legislate for the District at any time.

US-DE.note: A municipality with at least 1,000 residents that amends its charter under this chapter gains every power the General Assembly could grant and that no statute denies; smaller towns and those that have not amended keep only their charter powers.

US-FL.cite: Fla. Const. art. VIII, § 2(b); Fla. Stat. § 166.021
US-FL.note: All municipalities may exercise any power for municipal purposes except when expressly prohibited by law, and the statute removes judicially imposed limits.

US-GA.cite: Ga. Const. art. IX, § II, ¶ II; O.C.G.A. § 36-35-3
US-GA.note: By statute, cities may adopt reasonable ordinances on their affairs where general law makes no provision and that are consistent with the constitution; counties hold home rule directly under the constitution.

US-GU.note: Guam's village mayors hold only listed administrative duties (streets, sanitation, census, emergency help) and have no general legislative power, so every local power is delegated by the territory.

US-HI.note: Hawaii has no incorporated cities, and its counties exercise only the powers conferred under general laws; their charters control structure and organization, not residual lawmaking power.

US-IA.cite: Iowa Code § 364.1; Iowa Const. art. III, § 38A
US-IA.note: Every city may exercise any power it deems appropriate unless expressly limited by the constitution or inconsistent with state law.

US-ID.note: Every city may exercise all powers of local self-government in city affairs that are not specifically prohibited by or in conflict with state law.

US-IL.note: Home-rule municipalities (automatically those over 25,000 residents, others by referendum) may exercise any power not specifically prohibited by state law, while non-home-rule municipalities have only granted powers.

US-IN.note: Indiana's counties, cities and towns are exempt from Dillon's Rule, which applies there only to townships. The source is only the Wikipedia table's comment, because the Indiana Code site returned only a script shell.

US-KS.note: All cities may determine their local affairs and government, subject to uniform state laws, and their powers are construed to give them the largest measure of self-government. The source is a Wikisource copy because state hosts refused.

US-KY.note: Every city may exercise any power in furtherance of a public purpose that does not conflict with the constitution or a statute.

US-LA.note: Home-rule-charter governments may exercise any power not denied by general law, and a noncharter government gains the same power if its voters approve; otherwise it has only the powers the law grants.

US-MA.note: Every city and town may exercise any power the General Court could confer that is not inconsistent with its laws and not denied by the local charter.

US-MD.cite: Md. Const. art. XI-E; Md. Code, Local Gov't § 5-202
US-MD.note: Municipalities hold constitutional home rule and a general grant to adopt ordinances for good government, public safety, health and welfare; this is a general-welfare grant rather than an express 'any power not denied' clause.

US-ME.note: Every municipality may exercise any power the Legislature could confer that is not denied expressly or by clear implication.

US-MI.cite: Mich. Comp. Laws § 117.4j(3); Mich. Const. art. 7, § 22
US-MI.note: Home-rule cities (all Michigan cities) may exercise all municipal powers, whether or not enumerated, subject to the constitution and general law; townships remain under Dillon's Rule.

US-MN.cite: Minn. Stat. § 410.07; Minn. Const. art. XII, § 4
US-MN.note: Home-rule charter cities, which include Minneapolis and Saint Paul, may regulate all local municipal functions as fully as the legislature could; statutory cities, which are most cities by count, hold only granted powers.

US-MO.note: Charter cities hold every power the General Assembly could confer unless the charter or a statute limits or denies it; noncharter cities have only statutory powers.

US-MP.cite: N. Mar. I. Const. art. VI, § 7(a)
US-MP.note: Municipal councils' powers extend to all matters of a predominantly local nature not preempted by the Commonwealth Legislature, but their listed powers are budget and confirmation duties. The source is a Wikisource copy that could not be checked against cnmilaw.org, which returned only a script shell.

US-MS.note: Municipalities may adopt any order, resolution or ordinance on municipal affairs, property and finances that is not inconsistent with the constitution or general law, though they cannot levy taxes or issue bonds without specific authority.

US-MT.note: Only local governments that adopt a self-government charter may exercise any power not prohibited; general-power governments have narrower powers.

US-NC.note: City powers must still come from a grant; the statute only requires broad construction of granted powers and their reasonably necessary supplements.

US-ND.note: Home-rule cities hold self-government only 'within the powers enumerated' in the statute's list, and only as their charters include them.

US-NE.note: Only cities over 5,000 may frame a home-rule charter, and only Lincoln and Omaha have one; the constitutional text is a charter grant 'subject to the constitution and laws', and every other city lives under Dillon's Rule.

US-NH.note: Towns may adopt bylaws only on the subjects the statute lists, so Dillon's Rule governs.

US-NJ.note: The constitution orders liberal construction of municipal and county powers in their favor, including implied and incidental powers, and New Jersey is usually classed as a home-rule state; the general police-power statute could not be fetched.

US-NM.note: New Mexico's home-rule municipalities hold broad powers, while the others keep only granted powers. The only source available is Wikipedia's table, because nmonesource.com and the Secretary of State's copy of the constitution could not be fetched.

US-NV.note: Nevada keeps Dillon's Rule, modified since 2015 to give city governing bodies implied power over matters of local concern; those matters exclude statewide interests. The brief's definition classes this as Dillon's Rule; see conflicts.

US-NY.note: Every local government may adopt local laws relating to its property, affairs or government that are consistent with the constitution and general law. The source is a Wikisource copy as of 2004; this clause has been unchanged since 1963.

US-OH.note: All municipalities hold all powers of local self-government and may adopt local police regulations that do not conflict with general laws.

US-OK.note: Cities over 2,000 may frame their own charter; the text is a charter grant 'consistent with and subject to' state law, and its broader scope comes from court doctrine on municipal affairs. Noncharter towns have only statutory powers.

US-OR.note: The voters of every city and town may enact and amend their own municipal charter, subject to the constitution and criminal laws.

US-PA.note: Only municipalities that adopt a home-rule charter may exercise any power not denied by the constitution, the charter or the General Assembly; most of Pennsylvania's municipalities have not adopted one.

US-PR.cite: Código Municipal de Puerto Rico (Ley 107-2020), arts. 1.007, 1.008, 1.010
US-PR.note: Municipalities may order, regulate and resolve whatever is necessary or convenient for local needs, and their listed powers are non-exclusive and construed liberally; the autonomy they exercise is conferred by the Legislative Assembly. See conflicts.

US-RI.note: Every city and town has self-government in all local matters and may enact local laws on its property, affairs and government consistent with state law.

US-SC.note: Every municipality may legislate on any subject it finds necessary and proper for its security, general welfare and good government, consistent with the constitution and general law.

US-SD.note: Only a chartered (home-rule) county or city may exercise any legislative power not denied by its charter, the constitution or general law; few municipalities have adopted a charter.

US-TN.note: Tennessee home rule means only that the 14 home-rule cities control their own charters and are shielded from private acts; it does not grant residual powers, and most cities hold only statutory powers.

US-TX.note: Home-rule municipalities (cities over 5,000 that adopt a charter) have full power of local self-government; general-law cities have only granted powers.

US-UT.note: Municipalities have a broad general-welfare power to pass ordinances for the safety, health, prosperity and order of their residents, and the Utah Supreme Court rejected Dillon's Rule in State v. Hutchison (1980).

US-VA.note: Virginia is a Dillon's Rule state: a locality may act only where the General Assembly has clearly granted authority. See conflicts about Va. Code § 15.2-1102.

US-AK.note: One year: a former legislator may not lobby the legislature for one year after leaving.

US-AL.note: Two years after the elected term: a former legislator may not lobby for a fee before the legislative body he or she served for two years after the term of office ends, even if he or she left early.

US-AR.cite: Ark. Ethics Comm'n Rules on Lobbyist Registration and Reporting § 517(b) (Ark. Code Ann. § 21-8-601 et seq.)
US-AR.note: Two years after the term ends: a former member of the General Assembly elected on or after 11/4/2014 may not register as a lobbyist until two years after the end of the term (source is the Ethics Commission rule text revised 1/31/2020).

US-AS.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the most common answer among the 3 territories read for this question (2 answer no), because this place's own law could not be read.
US-AS.note: Tried: American Samoa Code Annotated at https://asbar.org/ (HTTP 403 bot block, section search unreachable); https://www.asbar.org/ (no connection); web.archive.org (no snapshot); https://www.americansamoa.gov/ (script-rendered site with no code text); constituteproject.org (404).

US-AZ.note: No cooling-off period on lobbying the Legislature: the 12-month post-service bar covers only matters decided through administrative discretion, and the lobbying article (§§ 41-1231 to 41-1239) has no section on former legislators.

US-CA.note: One year: a former Member of the Legislature may not lobby the Legislature for pay for one year after leaving office (a member who resigns is barred until one year after that session adjourns).

US-CO.note: Two years: a former member of the General Assembly may not represent others for pay before any member of the General Assembly or statewide elected officeholder for two years after leaving office.

US-CT.note: No cooling-off period for legislators: the one-year post-service bar covers former executive branch and quasi-public officials; a former legislator is barred from lobbying only after a corruption-related felony conviction.

US-DC.note: The lobbying part of the Ethics Act only bars a public official from being a lobbyist while in office, and it sets no waiting period for former Councilmembers.

US-DE.note: One year: a former member of the General Assembly may not lobby for pay for one year after leaving office (79 Del. Laws c. 427).

US-FL.note: Six years: a former legislator may not lobby the Legislature or any state agency for pay for six years after leaving office (the older two-year bar on representing others before one's former body also remains).

US-GA.note: One year: a former member of the General Assembly may not register as a lobbyist or lobby for one year after leaving office, unless he or she stays employed in state government.

US-GU.note: Two years: a former legislator may not act as a lobbyist for two years after the end of his or her last term.

US-HI.note: One year: for 12 months after leaving, a former legislator may not represent anyone for pay on matters involving official action by the Legislature (State Ethics Commission guide).

US-IA.note: Two years: a former member of the General Assembly may not become a lobbyist within two years after leaving service.

US-ID.cite: Idaho Code tit. 74, ch. 7 (Lobbying Disclosure); ch. 4 (Ethics in Government)
US-ID.note: No cooling-off period: Idaho's lobbying and ethics chapters contain no waiting period before a former legislator may register as a lobbyist.

US-IL.note: Six months: a former member of the General Assembly may not do state-level lobbying in a General Assembly in which he or she served until six months after leaving office.

US-IN.note: One year: a former member of the General Assembly may not register as a legislative lobbyist or work as a legislative liaison for 365 days after leaving (Lobby Registration Commission guidance).

US-KS.note: No cooling-off period found: the state governmental ethics and lobbying article has no section restricting former legislators from lobbying; its post-service rule (§ 46-233) covers only contract-related employment.

US-KY.note: Two years: a former legislator may not be a legislative agent (lobbyist), other than for a public agency, until two years after leaving office.

US-LA.note: Two years: a former elected official, which includes a legislator, may not assist another person for pay in any transaction or appearance involving his or her former agency (for a legislator, the Legislature) for two years after leaving (Board of Ethics summary).

US-MA.note: One year: a former member of the General Court may not act as a legislative agent before the body he or she served for one year after leaving.

US-MD.note: One year: a former member of the General Assembly may not assist or represent another party for pay in a matter that is the subject of legislative action for one year after leaving office.

US-ME.note: One year: a former Legislator may not engage in compensated lobbying until one year after his or her term ends (in this form since the 130th Legislature convened in December 2020).

US-MI.note: No cooling-off period on 1/1/2026: only a legislator who resigned early was barred from paid lobbying for the rest of the term. 2026 Public Act 74 (effective 7/27/2026) adds a two-year ban for members whose terms begin on or after 1/1/2027.

US-MN.note: No cooling-off period found: Minnesota's lobbying and ethics chapter lets former legislators register as lobbyists without a waiting period.

US-MO.note: Two years after the last session served: a former member of the General Assembly may not serve or register as a paid lobbyist until two calendar years after the end of the last session in which he or she served.

US-MP.note: The Ethics Act bars a former official only from matters he or she personally handled (plus a one-year bar on business transactions), and the lobbying law sets no waiting period for former legislators.

US-MS.note: Mississippi bars a former public servant only from paid work on a matter he or she personally handled in office, and no fixed waiting period for former legislators to lobby was found.

US-MT.note: Two years: a person who served as a state legislator in the previous 24 months may not be licensed as a lobbyist (voter-approved I-153, 2006).

US-NC.note: Six months or the end of the session, whichever is later: a former legislator may not register as a lobbyist before the later of the close of the session in which he or she served or six months after leaving office.

US-ND.note: Two years: an elected public official, including a legislator, may not be a lobbyist for two years after leaving office (voter-approved Measure 1, 2018).

US-NE.cite: Neb. Rev. Stat. ch. 49, art. 14 (Nebraska Political Accountability and Disclosure Act)
US-NE.note: No cooling-off period found: none of the lobbying or conflict-of-interest sections of the Political Accountability and Disclosure Act restricts former legislators from lobbying.

US-NH.note: No cooling-off period for legislators: the six-month post-service lobbying bar covers only executive branch officials and classified employees, and the lobbying and legislative ethics chapters set none for former legislators.

US-NJ.note: One year: a former member of the Legislature may not register as a governmental affairs agent (lobbyist) for one year after leaving office.

US-NM.cite: N.M. Const. art. IV, § 28; NMSA 1978, §§ 10-16-9, 2-11-1 et seq.
US-NM.note: The State Ethics Commission summary of ethics law for legislators lists no lobbying bar after leaving office, only limits on state contracts and civil offices for one year.

US-NV.note: Until the end of the next session: a former Legislator may not be paid to lobby until the final adjournment of the next regular session after leaving office (enacted 2015; narrow exception for an in-house employee whose job is mostly not lobbying).

US-NY.note: Two years: a former member of the Senate or Assembly may not be paid to promote or oppose legislation before either house for two years after leaving.

US-OH.note: One year: a former member of the General Assembly may not represent anyone on any matter before the General Assembly or its committees for one year after leaving.

US-OK.cite: Okla. Const. art. XXIX; Okla. Admin. Code tit. 257 (Ethics Rules)
US-OK.note: Weak: not in the Ethics Commission's 2025 annotated rules (which govern lobbying) or its 2021 compilation of ethics statutes and constitutional provisions; neither sets a waiting period before a former legislator may lobby.

US-OR.note: One year: a former member of the Legislative Assembly may not be paid for lobbying within one year after leaving the Legislative Assembly.

US-PA.note: One year: a former public official, which includes an elected legislator, may not represent anyone for pay before the governmental body he or she served for one year after leaving.

US-PR.cite: P.R. Laws, Ley 1-2012, art. 4.8
US-PR.note: The Government Ethics Act leaves legislators to their own chamber rules (art. 4.8), and no statute sets a waiting period before a former legislator may lobby.

US-RI.note: One year: a former official may not represent others before the agency he or she served for one year after leaving, and 'state agency' includes either chamber of the General Assembly.

US-SC.note: One year: a member of the General Assembly may not serve as a lobbyist while in office or for one year after leaving (applies to members elected after 12/31/1991).

US-SD.note: Two years: no elected state officer, which includes a legislator, may be paid, act or register as a lobbyist for two years after leaving state government (current text from 2017 session laws).

US-TN.note: One year: a former member of the General Assembly may not be a lobbyist during the 12 months after leaving office (Ethics Commission compilation of ethics laws, January 2024).

US-TX.note: No cooling-off period: the lobbying chapter lets former legislators register at once; it only bars a lobbyist from spending leftover campaign money on lobbying (§ 305.029).

US-UT.note: One year: a former member of the Legislature may not register or lobby for one calendar year after leaving office (Lobbying Restrictions Act of 2009; the section was amended again in 2026, effective 5/6/2026, keeping the one-year period).

US-VA.cite: Va. Code § 2.2-3104; Va. Code tit. 30, ch. 13
US-VA.note: No cooling-off period for legislators: the one-year post-service bar covers executive officials and designated legislative staff, not members, and the General Assembly Conflicts of Interests Act has no post-service provision.

US-AK.note: Alaska's state salary scale sections were repealed in 1970 and 1984; districts pay under local salary schedules.

US-AL.note: Alabama pays teachers on a state minimum salary schedule set each year in the Education Trust Fund budget; NEA's 2024-25 benchmark report lists Alabama among states with state minimum salaries or salary schedules (statute page not fetched).

US-AR.note: $50,000 minimum base salary for a starting teacher since the 2023-24 school year, under the LEARNS Act (Act 237 of 2023).

US-AS.note: The Department of Human Resources must use an official teacher payscale that follows the one appended to Public Law 30-20 (2008).

US-AZ.note: Weak: the governing board fixes employee salaries; no statewide minimum teacher salary found.

US-CA.note: Weak: each governing board fixes certificated pay; no statewide minimum teacher salary found.

US-CO.note: Weak: NEA describes Colorado starting pay as set by district bargaining and district salary schedules; no statewide minimum found.

US-CT.note: Chapter 166 sets no minimum teacher salary; boards of education negotiate pay with the teachers' union.

US-DC.note: The Code's teacher chapter has no salary schedule or minimum salary section; pay is set outside the Code.

US-DE.note: Statewide indexed salary schedule for teachers (the state-paid portion), with the base dollar amount set in the annual budget and local supplements added on top.

US-FL.note: District school boards adopt salary schedules; the state's Teacher Salary Increase Allocation funds raises but sets no enforceable statutory minimum salary.

US-GA.note: Georgia pays teachers on the State Board of Education's state salary schedule (O.C.G.A. § 20-2-212); NEA's 2024-25 benchmark report lists Georgia among states with state minimum salaries or salary schedules (statute page not fetched).

US-GU.note: The Uniform Position Classification and Salary Administration Act sets the pay schedule for Department of Education teachers, with step 1 as the pay for initial employment; the teacher plan reproduced in the Code dates from the 2014 pay study.

US-HI.note: The teachers' salary schedule is negotiated under section 89-9, so no statute fixes a minimum; only substitute pay has a legal floor.

US-IA.note: $50,000 for a starting teacher from the 2025-26 school year ($47,500 in 2024-25).

US-ID.note: No full-time teacher may be paid less than the minimum on the state career ladder; the first residency cell was $41,500 in 2024-25 and is adjusted for 2025-26.

US-IL.note: School boards must pay full-time teachers at least $40,000 for 2023-24, raised each year by the consumer price index (in force on 1/1/2026).

US-IN.note: The old statutory minimum, IC 20-28-9-1, was repealed in 2011; each school corporation adopts a local compensation plan with its own salary range.

US-KS.note: Weak: teacher salaries are negotiated locally under the professional negotiations act; no statewide minimum found.

US-KY.note: When the biennial budget contains a minimum statewide salary schedule, no teacher may be paid less than it; the dollar amounts are set in the budget bill, not in the statute.

US-LA.note: Each school system sets its own salary schedule; the old state minimum salary schedule sections were repealed by Act 1 of 2012.

US-MA.note: Only a local-option floor ($18,000 or $20,000) that applies if a school committee and appropriating authority vote to adopt it; no statewide mandate.

US-MD.note: Enacted but not yet in force on 1/1/2026: the Blueprint sets a $60,000 minimum teacher salary beginning 7/1/2026 (2026-27 school year).

US-ME.note: $40,000 minimum salary for certified teachers since the 2022-23 school year.

US-MI.note: Weak: district boards hire and contract with teachers; no statewide minimum found.

US-MN.note: Weak: salary is set in district contracts and bargaining; no statewide minimum found.

US-MO.note: $40,000 for a starting teacher from the 2025-26 school year (it was $25,000 through 2024-25), with inflation adjustments from 2028-29.

US-MP.note: The Board of Education writes teacher pay rules by regulation, merit based and subject to funds, so no statute sets a minimum salary.

US-MS.note: Mississippi pays teachers on a state salary schedule (Miss. Code § 37-19-7), raised in 2022 to about $41,500 for a starting teacher; NEA's 2024-25 benchmark report lists Mississippi among states with state minimum salaries (statute page not fetched).

US-MT.note: Weak: trustees contract with teachers; the state's starting-pay incentive program sets no mandatory minimum.

US-NC.note: State-allotted teachers are paid on the State salary schedule adopted in the budget act; the dollar amounts are set there, not in the statute.

US-ND.note: Weak: salaries are negotiated by district boards and teacher units; no statewide minimum found.

US-NE.note: Weak: teacher pay is bargained locally, with the Commission of Industrial Relations setting comparable wages in disputes; no statewide minimum found.

US-NH.note: Weak: districts set teacher pay and report average salaries; no statewide minimum found.

US-NJ.note: $18,500 statutory minimum for a full-time teacher, unchanged since 1985 and far below actual pay.

US-NM.note: $50,000 minimum for a level one (starting) teacher since Senate Bill 1 of 2022, with higher tiers for level two and three.

US-NV.note: A statutory commission studies whether districts should use a minimum salary scale, which confirms none is required; districts set pay.

US-NY.note: Article 51 of the Education Law only defines terms and prorating for teacher salaries; districts set pay by contract.

US-OH.note: $35,000 for a starting teacher with a bachelor's degree, on the state minimum salary schedule (as amended by House Bill 33, effective 10/3/2023).

US-OK.note: $39,601 in salary and/or fringe benefits for a starting teacher with a bachelor's degree on the 2025-26 state minimum salary schedule.

US-OR.note: Weak: ORS chapter 342 sets a minimum only for substitute teachers (ORS 342.610); districts set regular teacher pay.

US-PA.note: $18,500 statutory minimum for a full-time teacher since the 1988-89 school term, far below actual pay.

US-PR.cite: Ley 158-1999 (Carrera Magisterial); Ley 109-2008
US-PR.note: Law sets a basic salary of $1,750 a month for a full-time public school teacher hired from 7/1/2008; I did not check for later raises.

US-RI.note: The 'minimum salary schedule' section requires each district to adopt a step schedule but sets no dollar floor.

US-SC.note: Districts must pay at least the statewide minimum salary schedule set in the annual budget; NEA reports the minimum was raised to $47,000 for 2024-25.

US-SD.note: Enacted but not yet in force on 1/1/2026: from 7/1/2026 each district must pay at least the state minimum salary ($45,000 for fiscal 2025, indexed), enforced by aid cuts under § 13-13-73.9.

US-TN.note: Teachers are paid at least the annual state salary schedule; the 2023 Teacher Paycheck Protection Act raises the minimum starting salary in steps to $50,000 by 2026-27.

US-TX.note: Districts must pay classroom teachers at least the state minimum salary schedule set by the commissioner, by years of experience.

US-UT.note: The state funds educator salary adjustments by allocation; no statutory minimum salary.

US-VA.note: The Code sets only a goal of competitive pay and a biennial review; localities set salaries.

US-VI.note: The Code still prints a statutory Teacher Schedule (basic pay grades for teachers), last amended in 1970, so its dollar amounts are old and actual pay is likely set by union contract.

US-VT.note: Weak: teacher pay is bargained with school boards; no statewide minimum found.

US-WA.note: Full-time certificated instructional staff must earn at least $40,000, adjusted annually for inflation and regional cost since the 2018-19 school year.

US-WI.note: Weak: school boards contract with teachers; no statewide minimum found.

US-WV.note: Teachers receive at least the State Minimum Salary Schedule in the statute (A.B., zero years: $43,015 on the schedule effective for 2026-27), plus county supplements.

US-WY.note: Weak: teachers are placed on each district's own salary schedule; no statewide minimum found.

us-policy-positions:civil-family-communi.note: Yes where state or territorial law expressly bars discrimination for both sexual orientation and gender identity in both employment and housing; no where it leaves one out. Federal law already bars it in employment (Bostock v. Clayton County, 2020), so the question is what state law adds. Read from the Movement Advancement Project's map, data as of 9/28/2026; interpretations of 'sex' by a commission are not counted as law. Where the state is no, its cities may pass their own ordinance unless the state preempts them.

US-AR.note: The Intrastate Commerce Improvement Act bars a county or city from protecting a class state law does not, except for its own employees; the Arkansas Supreme Court applied it to void Fayetteville's ordinance in 2017.

US-IA.note: Sexual orientation only: Iowa's 2025 SF 418 took gender identity out of the Iowa Civil Rights Act from 7/1/2025.

US-MI.note: SB 4 (2023) wrote sexual orientation and gender identity into the Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act.

US-TN.note: The Equal Access to Intrastate Commerce Act bars a local government from adding any ground of discrimination beyond state law, except for its own employees.

US-UT.note: SB 296 (2015) added sexual orientation and gender identity for employment and housing, with religious exemptions.

US-VA.note: The Virginia Values Act (2020) added sexual orientation and gender identity to the Virginia Human Rights Act.

US-WI.note: Sexual orientation only, in employment and housing; gender identity is not listed.
